rationale: The entry's core is carried directly by the only texts printed with it (Jer 51:25 destroying mountain = Babylon; Dan 2:35 stone-to-mountain = everlasting kingdom) plus the explicit interpretive keys the chapter marshals (Dan 2:44-45; Rev 17:9-10 mountains = kings/kingdoms; Isa 2:2; Jer 51). These are definitional equations, not mere associations. The strongest counter (theophany/divine-presence site) accounts for Sinai/Zion narrative settings but treats the same definitional texts as secondary or exceptional and cannot unify the hostile-mountain and divine-mountain cases under one referent. The book's reading therefore explains the supplied evidence with fewer residual categories. Secondary claim (valley as opposite) is coherent with the high/low authority contrast drawn from the same texts and is not contradicted by them. Chapter-only extensions are ignored for scope.
book_core_identification: Mountain symbolically denotes a kingdom, nation, or high place as the seat of ruling authority.
chapter_only_objections: Reading 'flee to the mountains' (Matt 24 / Luke 21) as 'flee to the nations' rather than geographic refuge.
Reading the blazing mountain cast into the sea (Rev 8:8) strictly as a world empire falling into the peoples.
Reading the devil's 'exceeding high mountain' (Matt 4) as Babylon the Great.
Reading 'every mountain and hill made low' exclusively as the humbling of nations/cities.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Mountain primarily symbolizes the place of God's presence, theophany, and divine revelation (Sinai, Zion, Transfiguration mount, etc.), with kingdom/government as a secondary prophetic extension.
counter_core_identification: Site of divine presence, revelation, and God's dwelling or holy mountain (often extended to God's kingdom).
material_core_denial: Mountain does not symbolically mean kingdom/nation/seat of ruling authority; that sense is at best secondary, while the dominant sense is the locus of theophany and divine presence.
counter_case: Exodus 3, 19-20, 24 and 1 Kings 19 locate definitive theophanies and covenant-making on 'the mountain of God'.
Psalms 2, 48 and Isaiah 2 / Micah 4 treat Zion as YHWH's holy mountain and dwelling.
Synoptic mountains (Sermon on the Mount, Transfiguration, Great Commission) continue the revelation pattern.
Hebrews 12 explicitly contrasts Sinai and Zion as two mountains of encounter.
Kingdom imagery (Dan 2, Isa 2) can be read as an extension of the 'mountain of the LORD' rather than an independent definition of the noun.
book_explanatory_advantages: Matches the only places Scripture itself equates mountain with kingdom/king (Dan 2; Rev 17).
Unifies divine and hostile referents (God's mountain and Babylon as destroying mountain) under one political-authority sense.
Supplies a clear binary opposite (valley) that tracks high/low authority language already present in the cited texts.
Follows the book's stated method: prefer explicit interpretive keys over narrative setting.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Covers the large narrative cluster of Sinai/Zion/Transfiguration theophanies without re-reading them as political symbols.
Aligns with the most frequent devotional and liturgical use of 'holy mountain'.
Treats kingdom texts as natural extensions of Zion rather than requiring a separate primary sense.
